default: It is the twentieth day, in the third week.

The curse is still there, but it is plainly growing weaker. The turns in the market, the stillness and the emptiness, have become so rare that when one happens people notice it again instead of looking away. They notice because they have begun to expect that people will not stop dead in the street, which means they have begun to expect something better.

That is how a place like Crestfall gets better. Nothing dramatic happens. People simply begin to expect things again, and to believe, uncertainly at first and then more firmly, that tomorrow may be a little better than today.
You and [missing person] are part of what keeps them believing it. You go about the town every day doing the dull work of a place trying to remember how to run itself.

default.text: Every month somebody walks east to see that the seal is holding. This month it was Branch.
Lira keeps the herb stall on market days now.

choices.text: Go on.

text.default:
On the twentieth morning three people come out of the forest to the east gate. There are two men and a woman, thin and barefoot, blinking at the cobbles as if they had forgotten them. They went east months ago, and they don't know what month it is.

The soldiers already have them sitting on the ground. Vorne's sergeant wants them kept at the post until somebody can tell him what they are. Maret has come down from the camp with blankets and won't go back without them.
text.commander:
You have got into a routine. The mornings are for the account, with [missing person] and Pol. The afternoons are for the rest of it: the Compact's arrangements, the Covenant's smaller part in things, and the camp's growing place in the town.

Vorne has cut his garrison to twelve men, and the twelve are doing useful work: mending roads, handing out supplies, all the practical business of putting a town back on its feet, which soldiers are good at when nobody is using them for anything worse.

You and Vorne have found, by rubbing along in the same place, something that is not quite respect and is more use than friendship.
text.arcane:
The account is very thorough by now. You have spent three days with [missing person] on the sealing ritual, how the mechanism is made, and what the curse is and how it spreads.

Pol is the most valuable of you. Fifteen years of preparing have made her more exact than either you or [missing person] can be alone. Between the three of you, you are making something that is both sound scholarship and of real use.

When it is finished you will send copies to three different places of learning. It is not that you trust any one of them. It is that if the knowledge is in several hands, nobody can keep it to themselves.
text.ranger:
Every morning the land tells you how it is coming back.

On the seventeenth day there were two kinds of sparrow in the market square. On the eighteenth somebody saw a fox on the north road. On the nineteenth the cat that had been sheltering under the north porch went back indoors. On the twentieth there was birdsong before dawn.

The land is coming back, slowly, in the order these things always go: the smallest and hardiest first, and the bigger and more particular later.

You write it all down, every morning. The record will matter one day, when somebody needs to understand what the curse was and what the seal did.
text.cipher:
Three weeks into the new arrangements, things are settling into a shape you know.

Vorne is seeing to Crestfall's recovery with the Compact's money. Seriva has gone; she left quietly four days after the ritual and told nobody. Edric is still at the shrine, doing less than before, but what he does now is a priest's proper work.

The Rootless camp has the shakiest position of the three. It has been recognised, and that is real, but it is fragile. It rests on Vorne's goodwill, and Vorne's goodwill rests on Issa getting better.

Issa is getting better, slowly, but you can see it.

choices.text: Send them up to the camp with Maret.

default.text: Maret puts a blanket round the woman first. The sergeant writes it all down, slowly, so that you can see he is doing it. Then he lets them go.

choices.text: Let the Compact keep them at the post, for now.

default.text: Maret looks at you for a while. Then she gives the sergeant the blankets and walks back up to the camp on her own.

choices.text: Take charge of them yourself, and sign the sergeant's book.

default.text: You write your name in his book under the date, in the column for the officer responsible. He reads it twice. Then he stands his men back, and Maret takes them up the hill.

choices.text: Read what the forest left in them before anyone moves them.

default.text: You kneel in front of the woman and listen. The note is in her, faint, as a smell stays in a coat. It is fading, and there is nothing in her that could spread to anyone else. You say so, loudly enough for the sergeant to hear, and he lets them go.

choices.text: Read where they walked from, and show the sergeant.

default.text: You walk him fifty yards back along their tracks to where they came out of the trees. There are three sets side by side, and not one of them stumbles. "They walked out," you say. "They knew the way." He looks at the tracks a while, and lets them go.

choices.text: Find out what the sergeant is really afraid of.

default.text: It takes two questions. He isn't afraid of them. He is afraid of being the man who let them go, if it turns out badly. You give him a sentence to put in his report that makes it somebody else's decision. He writes it down word for word, and lets them go.

text.default: That leaves all the rest of the work, and there is more of it than there are hours. You will have to choose where to put yourself.

choices.text: Give yourself to the afflicted, the people the curse touched most deeply.

success.text:
You work with Maret and the camp's healers on a proper plan for looking after the afflicted while they mend.

The seal has stopped it getting worse, but it has not undone what was done. Lira is better, really better, but unevenly; some days she is nearly herself and on others she is a long way off. Issa is coming on steadily. Wren, who went east weeks ago, has not come back.

You find out about three others who went east and never came back, and you go looking for them. You find one of them at the edge of the forest, sitting quite still, but alive, and you bring them back.

The camp takes them in. When you arrive with them Maret looks at you and says nothing at all.

success_at_cost.text:
You work at it and get somewhere, but what the curse has left behind is more than any one person can deal with. You help the people in front of you, and accept that the ones you can't reach are out of your reach.

Ashenveld teaches you that again and again. There is only so much help in anybody.

failure.text:
It is beyond you, and not in the way you expected. You don't lack the skill. You lack the knowledge. What the curse has left behind will not answer to ways that ought to work.

At the end of a bad day Pol finds you and says, "Sit down. I want to tell you something about patience." And she does, for an hour, and it is the most useful thing anybody says to you in the third week.

choices.text: Finish the account. What you know must be kept, and shared.

success.text:
Two weeks of hard work with [missing person] and Pol give you something you had not expected: an account that is complete, and can also, somehow, be read.

[missing person] has fourteen months of what they saw, and Pol has fifteen years of learning, and you have a knack for putting things together. Between you, you write down what the ruins are, what the curse was, what the ritual needed, and what it did.

You send the first copy to the university in the capital, and the second to a scholar [missing person] trusts. The third you keep.

It is a secret no longer, and nobody can use it as a weapon for themselves alone.

success_at_cost.text:
The account is finished, but it takes longer than you meant, and it costs you. Some of the arrangements you were keeping an eye on went wrong while you were looking the other way.

That is what choosing costs. But the account is real, and it has gone out.

failure.text:
You don't finish the account in the time you gave yourself. [missing person] says, "It is not a deadline. This is Ashenveld. We have time now."

You are not good at not having deadlines. But you hear what they are saying, and you try to work at a different pace.

choices.text: Make the settlement permanent before Vorne's garrison leaves.

success.text:
You spend three weeks turning the spoken agreements into written ones.

The Rootless camp's recognition is set down in a charter for the region. It is not a Compact paper but a regional one, which means it will outlast Vorne. Edric signs as witness for the Covenant, Maret signs for the camp, and Vorne signs for the Compact. You witness it.

It isn't perfect. But it is written down, and witnessed, and the witnesses are alive and about in the world.

After the signing Maret stands outside the shrine in the autumn light and looks out over the market square and says nothing for a long time.

Then she says, "Thank you."

success_at_cost.text:
It is written down, but with conditions that make it less steady than you wanted. The camp is truly recognised, but the conditions give Vorne a bigger say in its affairs than you meant him to have.

Maret accepts the terms because the only other choice is nothing written down at all. You accept them for the same reason.

failure.text:
It isn't written down before Vorne's time runs out. He takes away most of the garrison with the agreement still standing, but only by word of mouth.

"We have always gone on word of mouth," Maret says. "We are still here." She says it more steadily than you could have, in her place.

text.default:
You are three days out of Crestfall.

The road has become ordinary, as the road into Ashenveld never was. There are no checkpoints, and no wrong silence, and no trees leaning in to watch you.

You and [missing person] walk through country that doesn't need reading. You find that more unsettling than you had expected.

You watch them getting used to the open world, and don't remark on it. They look at things, ordinary things: a market in a village, two men arguing over a fence, a dog asleep in the sun. They don't look anxiously. They look hard, like somebody who has had fourteen months without ordinary things and is learning what ordinary is all over again.

You let them learn it. You have nothing better to do.

choices.text: Go on.

text.default:
On the twentieth morning you wake and they are not beside you. You find them a hundred yards on, sitting upright in the middle of the road, facing east. Their eyes are open. When you say their name they look at you, and then at the road, and ask you how they got there.

The man on the east road told you the same thing had happened to him.
text.commander:
The road is a kind of halfway house between what you were in Ashenveld and whatever you will be next.

As you walk you think about the work you left unfinished. You made promises you can't keep from this distance. You will keep them by letter, and with the account when it is sent.

You wonder whether leaving was right, and you come to the same answer every time. It was not the only right thing to do. It was one right thing among several, and you did it, and now you walk.
text.arcane:
You are writing as you travel. It is not the account, which can wait. It is something else: what the ritual was like from inside, what the mechanism showed you, and what it really felt like for two people to want one thing together.

Nobody has ever written that down from the inside. As far as any record goes, you are the first person to have done the old sealing and lived to describe it.

You write carefully. Whatever words you choose will decide how it is understood for as long as the record lasts.
text.ranger:
As you travel you read the country, and the country reads as country should.

That sounds a small thing, and it is not. In Ashenveld, with the air poisoned, reading the land was a different kind of work. You had to think about what the curse might be doing to everything before you could understand what the land itself was doing.

Here the land is ordinary and it reads ordinarily. You find yourself grateful for it, in a way you would never have guessed three weeks ago.
text.cipher:
You have come out of all the scheming of Ashenveld on to an open road with [missing person], and the change is having effects you didn't expect.

You have nothing to manage. There is nobody to keep an eye on, no news to arrange, and no position to keep up.

You are not sure what you are without all that. You are spending the walk finding out.

choices.text: Tell them what you found.

default.text:
You tell them. They listen with their hands round a cup they haven't drunk from.

"East," they say. "Of course east." They put the cup down. "Wake me, if it happens again. Do not be kind about it."

choices.text: Say nothing, and watch for it to happen again.

default.text: You tell them they were walking in their sleep, which is true, and nothing else. For the next week you sleep lightly, with your boots on, and wake at every sound.

choices.text: Ask [missing person] about the fourteen months, and what it was really like.

default.text:
You walk most of a day, and they talk.

They tell you things they never told you in the ruins. They were not hiding them. There was no time, and it was the wrong place, and some things want an ordinary road and ordinary daylight to be said in.

They tell you about being lonely. It wasn't the hardship of it; they knew it would be hard. It was being alone in a place that seemed more there than most people are. In a way the ruins were company, even while they were dangerous.

"I talked to the Watcher," they say. "For months. I knew he could not answer. I talked anyway." They pause. "I do not know if that is sad, or only sensible."

"Bit of both, I should think," you say.

choices.text: Give them room. Let them come back to the world without having to tell you about it.

text: You walk beside them and you don't ask questions.
It is harder than it sounds. You are somebody who finds things out, and you are walking beside somebody who has fourteen months of things you don't know.

text.text: But you remember what they said in the Tallow, that they wanted just to be in the room with you, and you understand that they want the same now, only in a different place.
text.else: But you remember the night in the Tallow, when neither of you needed anything settled, and you understand that they want the same now, only in a different place.

text: You walk. The road is good and the weather holds, and Ashenveld falls further behind you at a walking pace.

choices.text: Keep watch, as you would on campaign.

default.text: You split the night into watches and keep both yourself. On the fourth night you see them sit up, and stand, and turn east, and you put a hand on their shoulder before they can take the first step. They wake, and know at once what happened.

choices.text: Listen for the note in them.

default.text: You sit beside them while they sleep, and listen. It is there, very faint, the note from under the chamber, running through them like a hair through a loaf. It isn't the curse. It is the place where they spent fourteen months, and it wants them back.

choices.text: Read their tracks back from where they sat.

default.text: Their tracks run straight for a hundred yards, heel to toe, without any wandering at all. Nobody walks like that in their sleep. Something walked them, and it walked them east.

choices.text: Ask what they were dreaming, before they decide not to tell you.

default.text: "The chamber," they say, before they can stop themselves. "It was quiet. I was the only one there. It was the best I have slept in a year." Then they hear what they have said, and go white.

default: It is the twentieth day, in the third week.
You said a week, perhaps two. The second week is nearly over and the list isn't finished.

That is what Ashenveld is like. It always wants more than you planned for. Every job you finish shows you two more that needed doing, and every arrangement you put in writing turns up another that is less settled than it should be.
And you are not unhappy here, which you had not expected. The work matters to people you think well of, and it is hard enough to be interesting, and you are not unhappy.
There is a letter on your table. [missing person] has been writing every three days from whatever ordinary place they have got to. The letters don't ask you to hurry. They are simply there.
Then the letters stop. Nine days go by with nothing. The carter who brought the last one has been and gone twice since with nothing for you.
text.commander:
The work is real, and it takes as long as it takes.

You read the letter, put it with the others, and go back to the Compact's arrangements. You will finish when the work is finished. When you said a week, you meant until it was done.
text.arcane:
The account is very nearly finished. Two more days, perhaps three, and then you can go.

[missing person] writes about an ordinary afternoon in a village two days west of Ashenveld: what the light was like, what they ate, and what two people were arguing about at the next table. Reading it, you understand what it means that they are somewhere ordinary and you are still here.

You work faster. You are not careless about it, but you are quicker.
text.ranger:
The record of how the land is mending is done, and so is the teaching at the camp. Branch can read the signs now as you do.

What is left is the scheming, which is not what you are best at. But you do it, because it needs doing and you are here.

[missing person] writes about a forest they walked through, and birds you both know. You read the letter twice, and then go and find Maret.
text.cipher:
The arrangements are as firm as you can make them in the time you have.

[missing person] doesn't press you. They write about a market, and something somebody said, and a meal. They are telling you what ordinary is like, and asking you, without saying so, when you are coming to be ordinary with them.

You finish the letter and make a list of what is left. Four days, you reckon. You write back: four days.

choices.text: Leave now, with the work unfinished.

default.text: You give Branch the half-written lists and Aldous the keys, and take the west road that afternoon.

choices.text: Set a day for leaving and keep to it, whatever happens.

success.text:
You set the day four days off. You work as though it could not be moved, which means choosing what comes first in ways you never would if you had all the time in the world.

What you can't finish you hand on to people who can carry it on: Maret for the camp, Branch for keeping watch on the land, and Pol for the parts of the account still to be written.

On the fourth day you pack.

Aldous gives you bread for the road without being asked, and charges you three coins less than the posted rate. He doesn't say that you said a week.

success_at_cost.text:
You keep to the day, but it costs you. Some things are left less finished than you would like, and three of the lines crossed through in your list are not crossed through as cleanly as you would have wished.

You go anyway. A thing left unfinished is not the same as a thing left undone.

failure.text:
The fourth day comes, and there is something that can't wait another week, so you stay another week.

You write to [missing person]: one more week. They write back: I know. You will think about the patience in those two words for a long time.

choices.text: Admit what is becoming plain: you are staying in Ashenveld.

default.text:
You sit with the letter and, for the first time in a fortnight, you are honest with yourself.

You are not finishing the work so that you can leave. You are finding more work because you are not ready to leave. It is not the same thing at all.

You write back. It isn't the letter you meant to write. It is a different one, and an honest one. You tell them what you have realised, and ask what they want to do about it.

The letter goes west. You wait for the answer, and you work while you wait, because that is what you do.

choices.text: Hand the work to Branch with written orders, and go.

default.text: You write the orders out in full, as you were taught: what is to be done, by whom, by when, and what to do if it goes wrong. Branch reads them twice and folds them into his coat. "Go," he says. You go.

choices.text: Read their last letter again, for what it doesn't say.

default.text: The writing is wrong. It is theirs, but it isn't hurried. It is unsteady, the letters leaning and the pen pressed too hard at the start of every line, as if each word were an effort. They were ill when they wrote it. You leave within the hour.

choices.text: Ask the carters on the west road where they last saw a traveller alone.

default.text: The third carter remembers. At an inn two towns on there was a traveller who came in one evening and didn't come down the next morning. "Fever, they said." You are on the road before he has finished.

choices.text: Write to the innkeeper, not to them.

default.text: The innkeeper writes back by return of post, which tells you most of it before you have opened the letter. It is a fever, and it is mending. "Your friend asks me not to worry you." You leave the next morning.

text.default:
It is the twentieth day.

You have settled into a way of going on that has nothing to do with the person who has gone, and everything to do with the people who are still here.

You spend the mornings at the camp with Maret and Branch, and the afternoons in the town, at the Compact post or the shrine or the market, doing the work of rebuilding, which needs somebody who can go between all the powers in Crestfall without being swallowed by any of them.

You are good at this; you always have been. You are doing it alone, which is nothing new, and you are doing it in a place you care about, which is.

You feel [missing person]'s absence all the time. You carry it as you would carry anything you have decided to carry, knowing it is there and not pretending otherwise.

Maret looks in on you every three days or so. She doesn't make anything of it. She simply happens to be where you are, at the same time, sometimes with a cup of something. You let her.

choices.text: Go on.

text.default: On the twentieth day Branch and two others carry the Watcher in from the gate stones on a litter. He doesn't resist. Pol puts him in the tent nearest the fire, and he sits there exactly as he sat against the stone, with his knees drawn up and his face turned away.
text.commander:
Vorne thinks well of you, not warmly, but as one professional of another. He has seen what you did in the ruins, and in the talks, and in the three weeks since.

He offers you a post in the Compact's government of the region. It is not a soldier's post. He wants you as an adviser, with the Compact's money and its messengers and its reach behind you, all of which would make your work go further.

You think about what it would cost you and what it would give you. You don't decide today.
text.arcane:
Since [missing person] went, Pol has become the nearest thing you have to a partner in the work.

She is careful where you are ambitious. She checks you whenever you claim too much, with the exactness of somebody who has spent forty years telling the difference between what is known and what is only believed. Working with her is humbling in the best way.

The work you are doing in Ashenveld will matter. That is something, and you hold on to it on the days when you feel most what you have given up.
text.ranger:
The land is mending, and you write it down every morning.

On the twentieth day there are three kinds of bird in the market square, and the deer south of the forest edge are moving as they should. Yesterday Lira went to the market on her own for the first time, and came back with bread and a look on her face that was not happiness exactly, but was going that way.

You can see the work. That helps, on days when other things are harder to see.
text.cipher:
You work alone, and you are good at it. That is a strength, and it is also the thing you most need to watch. When you are clever enough to make being alone work, it is very easy for being alone to become permanent.

It is Branch, of all people, who says to you one afternoon, "You should write to them." He doesn't say who he means, and there is no need. "Not asking them to come back. Just writing."

choices.text: Write to [missing person]. Don't ask them to come back. Just write.

default.text:
You write.

It takes two tries. The first letter asks them to come back without ever using the words. You see it for what it is, and begin again.

The second letter tells them what Ashenveld is like in the third week: the birds, and Lira going to the market alone, and the light at this time of year, which is not as you remember it from before.

You seal it and give it to the post rider, and go back to work.

A fortnight later a letter comes from a town two weeks west of Ashenveld. They are well. They write about ordinary things, slowly, as though each one were new.

At the end they have written: I am glad you are there. I mean both things in that sentence.

choices.text: Spend time with Lira. How she mends is the plainest measure of what the seal has done.

success.text:
You and Lira sit in the herb garden every morning for a fortnight.

She talks more as it comes back to her. It doesn't come back all at once, or in any order, but as it does in somebody who has had the road between their thoughts and their words broken. Some days are clear, and on others she is behind glass.

On the twenty-eighth day she tells you a whole story without once losing the thread of it. It is from before the curse, when she was living in the village to the east, about a fair, and a certain person, and something funny that happened.

When she has finished she looks at you and says, "I haven't been able to remember that for two years." She doesn't cry. She is putting it away carefully, as the camp has taught her to do, holding on to it because holding on matters.

It is the best thing that happens in the third week.

success_at_cost.text: You spend time with Lira and it is good time, but she gets better more slowly than you hoped. Mending doesn't go in a straight line. Some days are worse than the one before. You learn to tell a day that is worse than yesterday from a day when she is not mending at all, which are not the same.

failure.text:
It is not a good day for Lira. You sit with her anyway in the herb garden, saying nothing, which is what she needs, even though it doesn't feel like much.

Branch, going by, says, "You are doing the right thing." It is so unlike Branch to say anything of the kind without being asked that you believe him.

choices.text: Give him a job to do, as you would a new recruit.

default.text: Every morning you put a basket of kindling beside him and tell him the fire will need it by noon. On the fourth day the basket is empty and the kindling is stacked by the fire, crosswise, as they stack it in Harrow.

choices.text: Sit with him and listen for what the ruins left.

default.text: The note in him is loud, louder than in anyone, and underneath it there is something very small. It is a tune that somebody's mother used to sing. You hum it back to him, badly, and his head turns.

choices.text: Walk him round the edge of the camp every morning.

default.text: You take his arm and walk, and he comes. After a week he stops at the same spot every morning, on the east side, where you can see down to the road, and looks at it.

choices.text: Watch what he looks at when he thinks nobody can see.

default.text: It isn't the forest, or the fire. It is Lira's hands, when she ties her knots. He watches them every time. You ask Lira to teach him, and she does.
